Bullwhip ripples in external assurance: supply chain risks and auditor responses
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how amplified fluctuations in supply and demand (the bullwhip effect) influence auditors’ risk assessments and pricing decisions. By examining whether operational instabilities spill over into external audit fees and disclosures, it aims to clarify the role of supply chain volatility as a key determinant in the audit environment. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on a large sample of Chinese listed firms, the authors construct firm-specific measures of the bullwhip effect by calculating the ratio of the volatility of production to the volatility of demand. These measures are then merged with annual audit-fee data and textual analyses of key audit matters (KAM) in audit reports. A quasi-natural experiment exploiting China’s intelligent supply chain policy is used to address potential endogeneity. Findings The results show that heightened supply–demand imbalances are significantly associated with higher audit fees, indicating that auditors perceive and price in this operational volatility as engagement risk. The findings also reveal that, under more pronounced bullwhip distortions, auditors devote greater attention to supply chain–related disclosures in the KAM section, suggesting that operational risks now occupy a central place in external assurance considerations. Originality/value By integrating a critical operational factor into traditional audit fee models, this study broadens the understanding of how real-side inefficiencies shape external assurance costs and disclosures. The evidence underscores the importance of supply chain dynamics in auditors’ risk evaluations and highlights how policy interventions aimed at stabilizing supply chain operations can mitigate upstream auditing expenses and informational frictions.

papers.title: Quarterly reporting timeliness as an early signal of reporting and internal control risk
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to explore the significance of quarterly report lag as a potential indicator of firms’ annual reporting timeliness and internal control issues, informing policymakers about the incremental value of quarterly reports beyond other well-documented attributes. Design/methodology/approach Following Blankley et al. (2014), the authors use a two-stage approach to estimate a quarterly lag model and then examine the incremental information embedded in the unexplained (abnormal) component of quarterly report lag (AQRL). Findings Based on a sample of the US firms from 2007 to 2023, the authors find that AQRL predicts annual report lag and positively relates to the likelihood of internal control weaknesses. Additional analysis shows that the informational value of AQRL is mainly concentrated among the firms with Big 4 auditors, suggesting that quarterly reporting delays are more informative when audit processes are more standardized and stringent. Originality/value This study responds to the call by Kajüter et al. (2022) that researchers should investigate the impact of quarterly reports on “the time needed to perform the annual audit,” contributing to both interim financial reporting and reporting timeliness literature streams. While prior research mainly focuses on the frequency, content and assurance of quarterly financial reporting, the authors concentrate on the timeliness aspect that conveys useful information about the auditor, the client and the reporting process.

papers.title: Delisting system reform effects on avoidance behavior and audit reporting: insights from China’s market
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the effects of the latest delisting system reform, implemented in 2020 in China, on avoidance behaviors and audit disclosures among firms facing delisting risk. Design/methodology/approach The study uses the difference-in-differences model to empirically test panel data of China’s A-share-listed companies from 2018 to 2022, comparing observations before and after the reform. As a governance mechanism, changes in audit opinions are also analyzed. Findings The findings indicate that during the post-reform period analyzed, accrual-based earnings management increased while real earnings management remained stable. In addition, the likelihood of companies facing delisting risk receiving nonstandard audit opinions increased significantly, although there was no notable change in key audit matter disclosures. The results suggest that among the changes in the reform, although the cross-application of audit opinions and profit indicators is improving risk disclosure, further regulatory refinements are necessary to curtail delisting avoidance behavior. Originality/value The study provides systematic evidence on the reform’s aggregate impact, investigating its policy effects and focusing on common problems that require urgent solutions. The findings offer generalizable conclusions with significant implications for regulators assessing the policy’s overall effectiveness and for investors evaluating market-wide financial reporting quality to help enhance the capital market system.

papers.title: The Effects of Expanded Analyst Ownership Disclosure on Nonprofessional Investors’ Judgments and Decision-Making
papers.abstract: This study examines how expanded analyst ownership disclosures affect nonprofessional investors’ confidence in analyst recommendations and on their subsequent capital allocation decisions. In an experimental setting we manipulate information regarding the magnitude and duration of the analyst’s ownership position in a recommended stock. We find that investor confidence in analyst recommendations is significantly lower when analysts provide expanded disclosures, indicating that additional details heighten investor sensitivity to potential conflicts of interest in analysts’ recommendations. Consistent with attribution theory’s discounting principle, nonprofessional investors’ confidence is lowest when analysts disclose a large, short-term ownership position. We also document that investor confidence mediates the relation between analyst ownership disclosures and investors’ capital allocation decisions. Collectively, our findings provide evidence that expanded ownership disclosures influence both investor perceptions and behavior, offering support for regulatory initiatives aimed at enhancing analyst ownership transparency.

papers.title: Caught in the crossfire: Geopolitical risk and firm performance, and the lifeline of risk management and sustainability strategies
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to test the adverse impact of geopolitical risk (GP_RISK) on firm performance and to examine whether risk management and sustainability strategies mitigate this relationship in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries. Design/methodology/approach The study sample comprises 6140 firm-year observations from non-financial listed firms from 2013 to 2024. Consistent with prior studies, the study uses a system GMM estimator to address endogeneity and heterogeneity issues in panel data, ensuring consistent and efficient estimates. Findings The study shows that heightened GP_RISK significantly reduces firm performance in the GCC, negatively affecting both return on assets (ROA) and Tobin’s Q. The adverse effect is stronger for ROA, indicating that geopolitical shocks transmit more immediately through operational channels, including higher adjustment costs, supply-chain disruptions and operational inefficiencies. The negative impact on Tobin’s Q reflects investors’ concerns regarding future performance and risk exposure. The findings further show that geographical diversification (GEO_DIV) intensifies the adverse effect of GP_RISK, while hedging does not significantly mitigate it. In contrast, environmental, social and governance performance reduces the negative impact of GP_RISK, driven primarily by the governance dimension. Originality/value This study contributes to research on GP_RISK and firm-level dynamics in the emerging GCC context. It integrates political risk, risk management and stakeholder theories to explore the relationship between GP_RISK and firm performance and to evaluate the shielding effect of risk management and sustainability strategies. The research offers several important theoretical and practical implications for emerging economies.

papers.title: Financial support or innovation hindrance? Impact of venture capital’s discounted subscription in private placements on corporate innovation
papers.abstract: Purpose Venture capital (VC) participation in private placements may support innovation, but high subscription discounts can distort investor incentives and discourage long-term innovation. This study aims to examine how subscription discounts shape the innovation effects of VC participation. Design/methodology/approach Using China A-share listed firms from 2006 to 2023, this study examines the mechanisms and economic consequences of VC participation and subscription discounts in private placements. Findings VC participation in discounted private placements significantly weakens firms’ innovation capabilities. This effect operates through reduced R&D investment and increased inefficient investment and is more pronounced under greater information asymmetry. It is also stronger for mature and industry-focused VC investors, firms located in regions with greater capital concentration, growth-stage firms and financially constrained firms. Further analyses indicate that VC investors subscribing at higher discounts exhibit a stronger financial orientation. Under low-discount conditions, better innovation performance is associated with a lower likelihood of subsequent VC divestment, whereas this relationship disappears under high-discount conditions. Discounted subscriptions by VC investors also impair firms’ long-term stock market performance. Originality/value This study extends the VC short-termism literature by identifying entry-stage pricing as a determinant of VC incentives and corporate innovation.

papers.title: Can ChatGPT be skeptical? A case-based evaluation of generative AI in financial statement auditing
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how effectively GenAI (ChatGPT) displays professional skepticism characteristics in external audit tasks, as insufficient skepticism may impair audit quality and heighten the risk of audit failure. Design/methodology/approach ChatGPT is evaluated using four audit tasks representing common judgment-oriented audit procedures. Three experienced external auditors independently assessed ChatGPT’s responses using a structured professional skepticism assessment. Findings ChatGPT appears to display varying levels of skepticism characteristics across audit tasks, with relatively higher levels in preliminary risk assessments and substantive analytical procedures and lower levels in going-concern evaluations. This suggests that it may be more effective in analytical tasks than in those requiring deeper professional judgment. Originality/value This study appears to be among the first to systematically assess whether a general-purpose reasoning GenAI tool can display characteristics associated with professional skepticism across different audit tasks. By applying an established skepticism framework, it provides a structured baseline for understanding where GenAI may support or fall short in audit judgment contexts.

papers.title: Does supply chain digitalization affect corporate tax avoidance?
papers.abstract: Purpose The impact of supply chain digitization on corporate tax avoidance is a critical yet under-explored issue in tax governance within the digital economy. Against this backdrop, this paper aims to conduct an in-depth analysis of the underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions governing the relationship between the two. Design/methodology/approach This paper uses data from Chinese A-share listed companies (2011–2022) and uses a two-way fixed-effects model to test for direct effects, as well as conducting robustness tests, mediation tests, moderation tests and heterogeneity tests. Findings Supply chain digitalization significantly inhibits corporate tax avoidance, and the alleviation of financing constraints exerts a positive mediating effect in this relationship. Public scrutiny reinforces this curbing effect, while management myopia weakens it. Furthermore, this effect exhibits significant heterogeneity across different firms. In terms of economic consequences, the curbing effect of supply chain digitization on tax avoidance further reduces corporates’ risk-taking and enhances their reputation. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this paper provides the first empirical evidence that supply chain digitalization curbs corporate tax avoidance. By examining moderating effects and heterogeneous roles, and by linking the reduction in corporate tax avoidance to subsequent risk-taking and reputational outcomes, this paper further extends the boundaries of the literature in relevant fields. These findings offer several policy implications.

papers.title: Ex-military CEOs and income smoothing
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether CEOs with prior military service engage in greater accrual-based income smoothing than their nonmilitary counterparts, and whether such smoothing enhances or diminishes the informativeness of current earnings and stock prices in predicting future firm performance. Design/methodology/approach Using a sample of 34,357 US firm-year observations spanning 1993–2022, the authors identify military CEO status through multiple biographical sources including BoardEx, Capital IQ and Marquis Who’s Who, and measure income smoothing as a composite factor score derived from three established proxies. The results are robust across multiple identification strategies addressing endogeneity concerns, including firm fixed effects, propensity score matching, entropy balancing and instrumental variable analyses. Findings Firms led by ex-military CEOs engage in significantly greater income smoothing. Importantly, this smoothing enhances the informativeness of both current earnings and current stock prices with respect to future performance, suggesting that military-trained CEOs use smoothing strategically as a signaling mechanism rather than opportunistically. Originality/value This study identifies military experience as a novel, psychologically grounded determinant of income smoothing, demonstrating that formative imprinting experiences outside the corporate domain leave enduring marks on executives’ financial reporting practices. The findings contribute to the earnings quality literature by showing that the intent and consequences of smoothing vary systematically with managerial background.

papers.journal: Accounting, Economics and Law: A Convivium
papers.title: Cryptocurrencies and the Future of Money as a Public Good
papers.abstract: This article engages with Digital Assets and the Law to examine the implications of digital monetary innovations, including cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, and CBDCs, for the institutional foundations of contemporary monetary systems. It argues that these innovations bring into sharper focus fundamental questions about the purposes of money and whether existing public-private institutional arrangements remain adequate to fulfil them. Rather than viewing crypto-assets as exogenous developments, the article situates them within a broader historical and political context, tracing their emergence to longstanding tensions in monetary governance. Focusing primarily on policy responses in Western economies, it argues that many have been predominantly conservative, seeking to preserve and adapt the existing monetary order rather than addressing the underlying tensions from which these innovations emerged. Instead, the article proposes assessing alternative monetary arrangements according to their capacity to strengthen money’s character as a public good. It concludes by outlining five possible future scenarios, evaluating each in terms of their implications for monetary governance and the broader public interest.

papers.journal: Accounting, Economics and Law: A Convivium
papers.title: Perspectives on Credit Ratings: A Response to Reviews on “Rating Politics”
papers.abstract: I would like to thank Matthias Thiemann and Yuri Biondi for organizing this symposium on Rating Politics and Jacqueline Best, Quentin Bruneau and Alexandra Ouroussoff for their generous reading and inspiring comments. In my response to them, I elaborate on the strengths and weaknesses of the “financial infrastructures” approach to credit ratings. I argue that this approach allows for better understanding the dependence of both states and markets on credit ratings and the counter-intuitive incentive structure that shapes rating agencies’ behavior. At the same time, this approach yields a structuralist argument that has limitations when exploring the role of ideational factors in credit rating decisions.

Ex-bureaucrats and ex-politicians: impact on bank financial reporting quality
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper investigates the associations of ex-bureaucrats and ex-politicians serving on bank boards with financial reporting quality using a sample of Turkish banks over the period 2007–2022. Design/methodology/approach We mainly perform ordinary least squares and logistic regressions to test our hypothesis and address the research question. To mitigate selection bias and endogeneity problems, we perform the Heckman two-stage selection model and system GMM procedures. To mitigate the omitted variable bias, we use a fixed effects estimator. Additionally, we constructed an alternative sample by excluding ex-bureaucrats without professional experience in accounting, finance, taxation, or other relevant fields. Finally, we created interaction terms using the ex-bureaucrat and ex-politician variables. Findings The findings indicate that ex-bureaucrat directors are associated with higher financial reporting quality, particularly through lower discretionary loan loss provisions, whereas ex-politician directors exhibit no consistent association with financial reporting quality. Additional analyses provide robust support for the discretionary loan loss provision results. However, the evidence for small-profit reporting is less robust, particularly in the bank fixed-effects estimations. Furthermore, the results remain robust when ex-bureaucrats whose public sector careers were unrelated to accounting, finance, or related fields are excluded. This finding suggests that the documented association is more closely linked to the relevant expertise accumulated during bureaucratic careers than to bureaucratic status per se. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by showing that the association between ex-bureaucrats and bank financial reporting quality appears to depend on the relevant expertise accumulated during their public sector careers, rather than on bureaucratic background per se. It also offers novel evidence on the heterogeneous implications of different forms of government experience for bank financial reporting quality.

papers.title: Guest editorial: Accounting, auditing and financial management under digital governance
Analysts’ use of toxic emissions data
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines whether financial analysts function as information intermediaries by incorporating Toxics Release Inventory (TRI) data into their assessments of firms' environmental risks, as reflected in earnings forecasts and stock recommendations. It further investigates whether analysts' forecast and recommendation revisions influence subsequent corporate environmental performance, thereby providing evidence on the effectiveness of the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA's) market-based regulatory approach. Design/methodology/approach Using a longitudinal sample of US publicly listed firms from 1997 to 2011, the study analyzes how financial analysts utilize TRI data in their decision-making processes. An event-study methodology is employed to examine how the EPA's annual public release of TRI data affects analysts' forecast accuracy and dispersion. The analysis also examines the economic implications of analysts' forecast and recommendation revisions for firms' future toxic emissions. Robustness tests are conducted using alternative environmental risk measures and industry-level analyses. Findings The results indicate that higher pollution propensity is associated with greater forecast errors and increased dispersion among analysts. Analysts respond to increases in pollution propensity by revising earnings forecasts and stock recommendations downward, and they revise them upward when pollution propensity declines. Importantly, these analyst responses are predictive of subsequent reductions in firms' toxic emissions, suggesting that analyst activity can exert real effects on corporate environmental behavior. Overall, the findings support the role of TRI disclosures in facilitating market-based discipline. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to US firms and TRI data up to 2011. Future research could investigate other forms of noncorporate disclosure and verifiable pollution data in global contexts to enhance the generalizability of the findings. Practical implications The study provides empirical support for the EPA's use of TRI disclosures as a mechanism to encourage environmental improvements through capital-market pressure. Policymakers and standard setters may further enhance the effectiveness of such disclosures by requiring more detailed and standardized environmental information in firms' management's discussion and analysis (MD&A), thereby enabling analysts to better identify and price environmental risks. Social implications By demonstrating that financial analysts incorporate TRI disclosures in ways that can shape firms' environmental behavior, the study underscores the social importance of public transparency in holding polluters accountable. Analysts' forecast revisions and stock recommendations can trigger market responses that incentivize greater corporate eco-efficiency, resulting in lower toxic emissions and improved environmental quality, thereby benefiting affected communities and reinforcing corporate environmental responsibility. Originality/value This study offers novel evidence that financial analysts incorporate nonfinancial, noncorporate TRI data into their analyses, highlighting their role as information intermediaries in an environmental reporting context. It demonstrates that analysts are able to parse the uncertainty inherent in TRI data and translate environmental risk into financial outcomes through earnings forecast and stock recommendation revisions. Additionally, the study documents tangible effects of analyst behavior on firms' pollution abatement efforts, contributing to the literature on environmental accounting, analyst behavior and market-based regulation, with important policy implications.

papers.title: The impact of top management team regulatory focus on accounting conservatism
papers.abstract: Purpose Drawing on regulatory focus theory, this study aims to examine how top management teams' (TMTs) motivational orientations (promotion versus prevention focus) influence accounting conservatism and further explores the internal and external situational conditions that shape this relationship. Design/methodology/approach Using textual analysis to quantify TMT regulatory focus from management discussion and analysis (MD&A) across Chinese A-listed firms, this study applies multivariate regression analysis to assess the impact of regulatory focus on accounting conservatism. Findings Our results show that promotion-focused TMTs are more likely to diminish accounting conservatism, whereas prevention-focused TMTs enhance it. TMT restricted stock (internal situational factor) attenuates both the negative effect of promotion focus and the positive effect of prevention focus on accounting conservatism. Analyst coverage (external situational factor) weakens the negative effect of promotion focus on conservatism while amplifying the positive effect of prevention focus. Further subgroup analyses reveal that the effects of TMT regulatory focus are more pronounced in non-SOEs and firms with lower ownership concentration and are significantly moderated by auditor industry expertise and product-market competition, highlighting the role of internal governance and external market factors as important boundary conditions. Originality/value This study introduces TMT regulatory focus as a novel psychological determinant of accounting conservatism, shifting the literature beyond observable demographic proxies to the motivational drivers of managerial reporting behavior. Furthermore, it identifies two actionable governance levers that interact with TMT motivational orientations, offering a more nuanced framework for corporate governance and compensation design.

papers.title: Stakeholder proximity and non-GAAP earnings disclosure
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines the relation between stakeholder proximity and firms’ use of earnings measures not prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), commonly referred to as non-GAAP earnings. Design/methodology/approach Stakeholder proximity is measured using both geographic proximity (urban location) and social proximity (social connectedness). Using a sample of US public firms from 2002 to 2020, we estimate regression models and conduct cross-sectional and robustness analyses to address endogeneity concerns. Findings We find that stakeholder proximity is significantly and positively associated with the likelihood of non-GAAP disclosure, with social proximity exhibiting a stronger effect. Cross-sectional analyses indicate that the relation is more pronounced when information demand and financial-reporting scrutiny are higher and also stronger when firms have greater reporting discretion or face greater performance pressure. Additional tests confirm that the results are robust to endogeneity concerns and are not driven by firms’ strategic orientation. We further show that market reactions to non-GAAP disclosures are stronger for firms with greater stakeholder proximity. Originality/value This study introduces stakeholder proximity, particularly social proximity, as an important determinant of non-GAAP disclosure and provides evidence that proximity influences both disclosure decisions and investor responses.

papers.title: When risk silences optimism: supply chain disruption risk and the reduction of abnormal managerial tone
papers.abstract: Purpose Amid intensifying geopolitical frictions and the trend toward de-globalization, supply chain disruptions have emerged as a salient source of risk for firms, yet their implications for managerial disclosure remain unclear. Our study aims to reveal the impact of supply chain disruption risk on managerial tone management during earnings communication conferences. Design/methodology/approach Using data on China A-share-listed firms from 2006 to 2023, we examine how, why, and when supply chain disruption risk affects abnormal managerial tone during earnings communication conferences. Findings Higher disruption risk reduces abnormal managerial positive tone. The effect operates through two channels: first, managers provide more detailed factual explanations in managerial communication, which increases informational density, as evidenced by shorter and more structured sentences, thereby constraining rhetorical and emotional expression; second, higher supply chain disruption risk raises inventory pressure, which suppresses optimism. The effect is more pronounced when investor questioning is intensive, stock prices are overvalued, or supply chain concentration is high. It is more pronounced among firms with greater trade credit supply or lower excess operating profitability. Originality/value Our study contributes to the literature by linking supply chain disruption risk with strategic disclosure practices, and it offers practical implications for enhancing supply chain resilience, improving disclosure quality, and strengthening market competitiveness.

papers.title: Tax Policy Uncertainty and Corporate Tax Strategies
papers.abstract: This paper examines how firm‐level exposure to tax policy uncertainty affects corporate tax avoidance. Using US public firms from 2002 to 2020, we measure exposure with the tax policy risk (TPR) index of Hassan et al., which captures the share of quarterly earnings‐call discussion devoted to risks surrounding tax policy. Firms with greater exposure to tax policy uncertainty exhibit lower effective tax rates: a one‐standard‐deviation increase in TPR raises tax avoidance by 2%–3% relative to the sample mean, and the relationship survives instrumental‐variable estimation, propensity score matching, and lead‐lag tests. Consistent with real options reasoning, in which uncertainty about domestic tax policy raises the value of relocating income to less exposed jurisdictions, high‐TPR firms shift more income abroad and operate more tax‐haven subsidiaries. The response is concentrated among financially flexible firms, firms with earnings‐management expertise, and firms with market power, and shareholders value tax avoidance more highly when tax policy uncertainty is high. Our findings identify tax policy uncertainty as a distinct driver of corporate tax strategies.

papers.title: Stakeholder Orientation and Stock Investors’ Response to Earnings Reports: Evidence from Stakeholder Constituency Statutes
papers.abstract: This study examines whether stakeholder orientation, which allows directors to consider the interests of stakeholders beyond shareholders, affects investors’ responses to earnings announcements, as measured by earnings response coefficients (ERCs). We hypothesize that stakeholder orientation increases ERCs by mitigating managerial opportunism and excessive risk‐taking. Exploiting the staggered adoption of constituency statutes across U.S. states as a natural experiment, we find that stakeholder orientation increases ERCs through these channels. We further show that investors in stakeholder‐oriented firms respond more strongly to earnings news even when underlying earnings quality is held constant, suggesting that such earnings are perceived as more credible. The effect is stronger in settings with greater stakeholder conflicts, weaker monitoring, and higher consumer orientation. Overall, our findings provide evidence that stakeholder orientation enhances investor responsiveness to earnings reports by improving both the credibility and informativeness of reported earnings.

papers.title: Work Division in Auditing: How Auditors Perceive and Interact with Work Started by Others
papers.abstract: Extant accounting research documents that the division of work among human colleagues can unintentionally harm task performance. Recent advances in accounting firms’ technological capabilities, however, have enabled a new form of collaboration between human auditors and sophisticated technological tools. This article summarizes a recent study by Pearson (2025), which examines variation in engagement and performance when auditors complete work initiated by a human colleague, a technological tool, or themselves. Key study findings indicate that dividing work with a human colleague significantly reduces engagement and harms performance compared to dividing work with a technological tool or work completed independently. This article discusses the implications of these findings, highlighting the practical benefits of technology-enabled work division, particularly for objective tasks, while also discussing the potential drawbacks of collaboration among human auditors. Data Availability: Data sharing is not applicable as no quantitative datasets were generated for this article. JEL Classifications: M42.

papers.title: Comments of the Auditing Standards Committee of the Auditing Section of the American Accounting Association on the PCAOB’s Standard Setting Agenda
papers.abstract: On June 23, 2026, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) issued a request for comment on its standard-setting agenda (PCAOB 2026). This comment letter summarizes the views of the participating members of the Auditing Standards Committee of the Auditing Section of the American Accounting Association. We recommend that the Board assign its highest priority to data, technology, and artificial intelligence; fraud; and going concern. We also recommend that the Board add complex estimates, fair value measurements, and specialist evidence to its research agenda with moderate-to-high priority; use economic analysis to evaluate scalability, competitive effects, and unintended consequences; avoid creating de facto requirements primarily through inspection and remediation processes; and pursue alignment with IAASB and ASB standards unless PCAOB-specific differences are justified by investor-protection benefits that exceed implementation costs.

papers.title: Comments of the Auditing Standards Committee of the Auditing Section of the American Accounting Association on the PCAOB’s Draft 2026–2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives
papers.abstract: On July 20, 2026, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) issued a request for comment on its 2026–2030 draft strategic plan goals and objectives (PCAOB 2026a). The Auditing Standards Committee (ASC) submitted this comment letter to the PCAOB, expressing our views regarding the goals and objectives. Overall, the ASC supports the goals and objectives and provides suggestions for refining them.

papers.journal: International Journal of Accounting and Information Management
papers.title: Financial reporting quality and investment efficiency: the moderating role of audit quality
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to analyze the influence of financial reporting quality (FRQ) and audit quality (AQ) on firms’ investment efficiency (IE) within an emerging market context and to explore whether AQ acts as a moderating factor in the relationship between FRQ and IE. Design/methodology/approach This study uses panel data from 291 non-financial listed firms in Vietnam covering the years 2014–2023, totaling 2,910 firm-year observations. IE is measured as the residual from an investment model based on growth opportunities. FRQ is created from three measures based on accruals and revenue, along with a composite FRQ index. The models are estimated using feasible generalized least squares (FGLS) and the two-step system generalized method of moments (SGMM). Findings Both FRQ and AQ positively influence IE, with AQ demonstrating greater robustness under SGMM. The interaction between FRQ and AQ is statistically significant and negative, suggesting a partial substitution effect. Research limitations/implications FRQ measurement methods may be subject to estimation errors, and AQ is constrained to a binary Big Four audit firms proxy. Potential self-selection bias and limited generalizability remain considerations. Practical implications Firms not audited by the Big Four audit firms are encouraged to strengthen their FRQ through timely and predictive disclosures. Simultaneously, regulatory authorities should enhance their oversight of audit practices and of IFRS implementation. Social implications Improving FRQ and AQ fosters transparency and efficient capital allocation. Originality/value This study offers new evidence from Vietnam, demonstrating that FRQ and AQ serve as partly substitutive governance mechanisms in emerging markets.

papers.journal: International Journal of Accounting and Information Management
papers.title: Information asymmetry and investor valuation of Egyptian firms: do corporate leverage and profitability matter?
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the extent to which information asymmetry affects corporate investor valuation, drawing on the pecking order, agency and signaling theories. Similarly, it examines how corporate leverage and profitability levels affect the relationship between information asymmetry and corporate value. Design/methodology/approach The study’s sample consists of Egyptian firms listed on the Egyptian exchange (EGX) 100 index from 2015 to 2022. A wide (narrow) bid-ask spread indicates high (low) information asymmetry. The corporate value of Egyptian firms is measured using Tobin’s Q ratio. This study also used the market-to-book ratio to assess the firm’s value. Findings The results reveal that Egyptian listed firms with high levels of information asymmetry, particularly those with wide bid-ask spreads, tend to experience a diminished market value. However, both financial leverage and firm profitability mitigate the inverse impact of information asymmetry on corporate value, highlighting their moderating roles in this nexus. Practical implications Egyptian firms should enhance transparency and reporting to improve investor confidence and market valuation. Firms with high information asymmetry can use leverage and profitability metrics strategically to signal stability and mitigate negative impacts on value. Likewise, policymakers should enforce stronger disclosure standards to foster market efficiency in Egypt. Originality/value Our study examines the relationships among corporate value, information asymmetry and the moderating effects of firm leverage and firm profitability. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first empirical study to investigate this nexus in Egypt, thereby extending the literature to a developing economy characterized by high information asymmetry.

papers.journal: International Journal of Accounting and Information Management
papers.title: Does the OCI information usefully predict accounting conservatism behavior? Evidence from US-listed companies
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate whether and how the other comprehensive income (OCI) amount explains firms’ future orientation toward accounting conservatism behavior. Whereas OCI provides incrementally useful and more transparent accounting information, the authors argue that a higher amount of OCI aggregate may also lead to a lower demand for accounting conservative practices. Design/methodology/approach To test the hypothesis, the authors develop a fixed-effect panel analysis involving a sample of US non-financial listed companies during a seven-year period from 2012 to 2018. Findings Coherently with the authors’ expectations, the results provide evidence that a higher amount of OCI aggregate significantly diminishes the future level of firms’ conditional conservatism. Additionally, further analyses reveal that the lowering of information asymmetry perceived by market participants is a valid channel through which such a relationship functions. Research limitations/implications The main limitations of the study arise whereas the inferences the authors made heavily depend on the chosen proxies’ validity for OCI information. Practical implications Overall, the authors’ study has important implications for both practitioners and investors, as it prompts the idea that they can predict certain accounting policies relying on the usefulness of OCI information, which consequently allows them to make more informed and economically relevant choices. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this would be the first research to document the relationship between OCI information usefulness and subsequent conditional conservatism behavior, under the spectrum of informativeness concerns.

papers.title: Corporate governance and HR ethics: case insights on compliance programs
papers.abstract: This study examines how compliance programs operate as governance mechanisms, shaping the ethical conduct of human resources over time. Drawing on Michel Foucault’s conceptualization of ethics, the paper analyses how different configurations of compliance practices influence employees’ moral subjectification. The study adopts a qualitative case study approach, based on 19 semi-structured interviews with organizational members holding governance, leadership, and operational roles in a pharmaceutical company operating under the Italian Legislative Decree (LD) 231/01, complemented by documentary analysis. The findings reveal a two-stage process. In the initial phase, the compliance program functioned primarily through the technologies of government, emphasizing control, monitoring, and sanctions. These mechanisms constrained employees’ discretion and fostered compliance, driven by fear of punishment rather than ethical engagement. In the subsequent phase, changes in leadership practices—particularly the role of the Compliance Officer—reoriented the compliance program toward enabling technologies that supported ethical reflection, autonomy, and self-regulation. As a result, employees increasingly perceived compliance as a resource for responsible decision-making rather than a coercive constraint. The study contributes to the governance literature by showing how the same compliance framework can produce different ethical outcomes, depending on how governance mechanisms are enacted and interpreted. This highlights the critical role of leadership in aligning control systems with the development of ethical self-governance.

The determinants of dysfunctional audit behavior in an emerging context: a cognitive approach
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to explore the external and internal determinants of dysfunctional audit behavior in the Tunisian context using a cognitive approach. Design/methodology/approach The authors’ methodological approach is based on a cognitive approach. The authors use the cognitive mapping method to analyze 12 auditors’ cognitive maps in Tunisia. A collective map was grounded through assembling the full individual maps. Findings Using the Decision Explorer software for this analysis, the authors find that time budget pressure, client importance, turnover intention and job burnout are the most significant factors that can lead to dysfunctional audit behavior among Tunisian auditors. Practical implications This study’s findings help audit firms to identify the most significant factors that increase the probability of engaging in dysfunctional audit behavior. Furthermore, this paper contributed to the researchers, auditors and educators in further understanding of the factors that lead to dysfunctional behavior among auditors. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this research is among the first to examine internal and external factors that contribute to dysfunctional audit behavior using a cognitive approach. This paper contributes to the literature on accounting by analyzing the determinants of dysfunctional behavior based on attribution theory.

papers.title: Sustainability integration in risk assessment and management accounting: insights from Iran
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to investigate the adoption of sustainability principles by Iranian firms in their strategic planning, risk management and management accounting (MA) practices. It aims to build a structural model that demonstrates how industry-driven, sustainable risk assessment tools can enhance organizational responsibility, adaptability and adherence. Design/methodology/approach The research adopted a survey approach, serving 103 Iranian companies from different sectors of the business world. To examine these relations of strategic planning, sustainable risk assessment tools and integration of sustainability in MA systems, structural equation modeling (SEM) was used. Procedural and statistical remedies were used to check and control the common method bias. Findings The findings indicate that enterprises using sustainable risk assessment instruments are significantly more advanced with respect to the inclusion of environmental issues in MA. Environmental and social risk assessments are highly determined by strategic planning, as sustainable risk assessment tools become an important mediator between the integration of sustainability in MA and global organizational sustainability performance. Yet, there are many companies without unit-level sustainability departments or that still report sustainability within the traditional accounting systems, suggesting enduring institutional and structural impediments. Originality/value In this early empirical research in Iran, the relationship between sustainability and risk assessment and MA is explored using SEM. By embedding the sustainability integration concept in a developing economy, this study supplements the limited literature on sustainable MA in a non-Western context.

papers.title: “Less is less” or “Less is more”? Financial constraints and green innovation in a global context
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the theoretically ambiguous relationship between financial constraints and green innovation. The resource-based view holds that financial frictions impede green innovation by restricting investment in costly, risky technologies (“less is less”), whereas the induced innovation hypothesis argues that these constraints can spur creativity and adaptive problem solving, thereby enhancing green innovation (“less is more”). Design/methodology/approach This study uses the ordinary least squares (OLS) method to analyze 2,750 firms across 44 countries for the 2005–2021 period. In addition, propensity score matching, firm fixed effects, change regression and lead-dependent variable techniques are applied to address potential endogeneity concerns. Findings Results show that financial constraints reduce firms’ green innovation, supporting the “less is less” hypothesis. The effect is more pronounced among firms in countries with higher economic development, weak national governance and lax environmental policy enforcement. Reduced environmental expenditure and poor workforce wellbeing channel the effect. Institutional ownership and strong corporate governance reduce the adverse impact of financial constraints on green innovation. Practical implications This study suggests how financial constraints hinder green innovation. Specifically, the conditions under which financial constraints undermine corporate responses to climate change are clarified. Originality/value Cross-country empirical evidence of the impact of financial constraints on green innovation is scarce. This study provides valuable insights by presenting comprehensive, cross-country empirical evidence. In addition, moderation analysis offers new insights into how various factors shape the relationship between financial constraints and environmental innovation.

papers.title: The challenge of comparability in sustainability reporting within the emerging standard-setting architecture
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to explain why standardisation does not necessarily produce substantive comparability in sustainability reporting and examines how the increasing concentration of standard-setting authority around institutions rooted in financial reporting may affect the conditions under which comparability enhances reporting quality. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual paper integrates insights from the accounting and sustainability reporting literature with a comparative documentary analysis of selected major reporting frameworks and guidance. It examines how comparability is conceptualised and operationalised across different reporting traditions and relates these approaches to the distinctive informational and measurement characteristics of sustainability reporting. Findings Sustainability reporting’s greater informational extensiveness and weaker calculative infrastructure amplify the risk that standardisation produces comparability in form without comparability in meaning. Institutional concentration is not inherently problematic, but concentration around institutions rooted in financial reporting may increase the salience of uniformity-oriented regulatory logics. Their translation is not deterministic; when reproduced without sufficient recalibration, however, they may suppress material contextual differences and weaken relevance and faithful representation. Practical implications The proposed framework helps standard setters calibrate common requirements across disclosure topics by identifying when standardisation supports substantive comparability and when it must be complemented by contextual or entity-specific information. Originality/value The paper reconceptualises comparability as a condition-dependent attribute of sustainability reporting quality. It argues that ex post comparability is endogenous to the ex ante representational choices through which information is selected, delimited and measured and develops five conditions – boundary equivalence, construct equivalence, contextual interpretability, measurement equivalence and temporal articulation – for assessing substantive comparability.

papers.title: Strategic pathways to agility: how dynamic management control systems, strategic management accounting and knowledge management foster organizational learning and adaptability
papers.abstract: Purpose In today’s volatile business environment, organizational agility (OAG) is critical for sustaining competitive advantage. This study aims to examine how dynamic management control systems (DMCS), strategic management accounting practices (SMAP) and knowledge management practices (KMP) contribute to the development of organizational learning capabilities (OLC) that enhance organizational agility. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the dynamic capabilities theory and knowledge-based view, data were collected via a cross-sectional survey of 161 Saudi medium and large firms from the manufacturing and service sectors. Structural equation modeling was used to analyze the hypothesized pathways. Findings The results reveal that organizational agility arises from the integrated effects of DMCS, SMAP and KMP through OLC. KMP enhances OLC, which fully mediates its impact on agility, whereas SMAP directly strengthens agility by improving decision quality and resource adaptability. DMCS influences agility indirectly by fostering the use of SMAP and enabling OLC, highlighting its role as an enabling infrastructure that strengthens the effectiveness of these systems. Overall, agility emerges through their complementary alignment, which jointly builds adaptive capacity. Practical implications For practitioners, the findings emphasize the need to align control systems, strategic accounting and knowledge processes to cultivate learning and improve agility. This paper offers actionable insights for organizations navigating dynamic markets and advances the theoretical understanding of agility’s antecedents. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by empirically validating an integrated framework that delineates the microfoundations of agility. It highlights the pivotal role of OLC as a mediator and reveals the complementary yet distinct pathways through which DMCS, SMAP and KMP operate.

papers.title: Beyond regulation: adaptive responses of nonregulated SMEs to mandatory CSR reporting
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether mandatory sustainability/corporate social responsibility (CSR) disclosure generates spillover effects beyond firms directly subject to regulation. While prior research focuses mainly on direct compliance effects, little is known about whether disclosure mandates reshape reporting practices among nonregulated firms, despite the relevance of this question for current debates on the scope of European Union (EU) sustainability regulation. Design/methodology/approach Using Sweden’s implementation of the Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD) as a natural experiment, the study exploits statutory size thresholds that distinguish directly regulated firms from nonregulated listed small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) within a common institutional environment. A generalized difference-in-differences design estimates reform effects for directly regulated Swedish firms and nonregulated Swedish SMEs relative to non-EU manufacturing firms, while using variation in SMEs’ distance from the thresholds to identify spillover effects. CSR reporting is measured using hand-collected annual and CSR reports and issue-level coding of substantive disclosures based on a SASB materiality framework. Findings Nonregulated SMEs close to the thresholds increase CSR reporting substantially following the reform, with stronger effects among firms with low pre-reform reporting levels. The findings indicate that mandatory disclosure can generate meaningful spillover effects beyond formally regulated firms and that firms near regulatory thresholds may respond strongly even when legally outside the mandate. Originality/value The study shows that mandatory CSR disclosure can reshape reporting practices among firms legally outside the mandate. It theorizes regulatory thresholds as institutional boundary markers that heighten visibility, stakeholder expectations and uncertainty about future inclusion, linking targeted transparency with spillover coercive and mimetic pressures beyond formal compliance boundaries.

papers.title: Cross framework alignment in mandatory ESG reporting: evidence from integrated reporting and SASB quality
papers.abstract: Purpose Fragmentation remains a central challenge in sustainability reporting, especially in the shift from voluntary to mandatory regimes. This study aims to examine whether Integrated Reporting (IIRF) quality aligns with sector-specific Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB) disclosure quality under Chile’s dual mandate (NCG 461). Although both aim to enhance transparency, they reflect distinct logics, holistic value creation versus financially material, industry-specific disclosure. Whether these logics translate into aligned practice under a mandatory setting remains unclear. Design/methodology/approach Using 290 firm-year observations (2022–2023), this study constructs formative, framework-anchored disclosure quality indices for IR and SASB based on item-level coding. This study estimates fixed effects association and interaction models to test complementarity versus operational independence, supported by standard diagnostics and robustness checks. Findings IR and SASB quality are weakly correlated, and the IR × SASB interaction term is statistically insignificant. The evidence supports a pattern of parallel disclosure rather than substantive integration. Firms appear to converge in form under regulatory pressure, yet narrative connectivity and sector material metrics remain loosely coupled. Results are stable across specifications. Research limitations/implications The analysis covers two reporting years under NCG 461, constraining causal identification and precluding dynamic panel models; findings are therefore associational and specific to an emerging-market, early-mandate setting. The SASB quality assessment relies on structured human coding without formal inter-coder reliability statistics. Future research should exploit quasi-experimental variation from regulatory thresholds or staggered International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) adoption, develop longer multi-year panels and incorporate replicated double-coding designs to strengthen methodological transparency. Practical implications Institutional consolidation alone does not produce substantive integration. Regulators should introduce standardized IR–SASB reconciliation schedules, mandatory linkage notes and staged assurance on narrative–metric coherence. Preparers need to redesign reporting workflows so each IR content element is explicitly anchored in SASB metrics, supported by clear data ownership and an integrated close process. Investors should not treat IR quality as a proxy for SASB quality but should request explicit reconciliations and linkage-focused assurance statements. Social implications Fragmented sustainability reporting obscures how firms manage material Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) risks, undermining stakeholder trust and the credibility of transition narratives. By documenting parallel disclosure under a mandatory regime, this study shows that formal convergence of standards does not automatically deliver decision-useful information for society, regulators or capital markets. Strengthening narrative–metric linkage, ESG data governance and assurance on coherence can enhance transparency, reduce greenwashing perceptions and support more informed capital allocation toward firms that genuinely integrate sustainability into strategy and long-term value creation. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study provides one of the first direct cross-framework tests of IR–SASB alignment under a mandatory dual-adoption regime. It introduces a typology of integration outcomes and offers implementation relevant insights for regulators, firms and investors in the ISSB era.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: Audit partner characteristics and key audit matters (KAMs) disclosure: evidence from Indonesia
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines the association between audit partner characteristics and the disclosure of key audit matters (KAMs) in Indonesia. Design/methodology/approach Using annual reports of firms listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) for 2022, this study manually collects KAM disclosures and employs content analysis based on both the number of KAM items and the total word count of KAM disclosures. The proposed hypotheses are then tested using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression analysis. Findings The results indicate that audit partners affiliated with reputable audit firms are positively associated with both the number and the extent of KAM disclosures. Furthermore, female audit partners tend to provide more comprehensive and detailed KAM explanations compared to their male counterparts. However, the evidence does not support the hypotheses suggesting that female partners disclose fewer KAMs or that busier audit partners provide fewer or less extensive KAM disclosures. Research limitations/implications These findings contribute to the growing body of literature on audit partner characteristics and audit transparency, particularly within emerging markets adopting enhanced auditing standards such as SA 701. Practical implications The study suggests that regulators and audit firms should carefully consider partner-level attributes, such as gender diversity and workload management when designing audit engagement assignments, as these factors may influence the nature and clarity of audit communications and contribute to more informative and transparent KAM disclosures. Originality/value This study contributes to the growing body of literature on audit partner attributes and KAM reporting by providing early empirical evidence from the Indonesian context. It highlights the significant role of gender and audit firm reputation in shaping audit reporting transparency under the enhanced auditing requirements of SA 701.

papers.title: Preparers’ and auditors’ views on the accounting for development costs capitalisation: an ambiguity aversion perspective
papers.abstract: Purpose Research and development (R&D) is characterised by an ambiguous information environment where future outcomes are unknown. While archival studies document a relative prevalence of expensing development costs, this study explores the views of preparers and auditors on the accounting for the capitalisation of development costs under International Accounting Standard (IAS) 38. Design/methodology/approach Semi-structured interviews were held with 11 preparers and 10 auditors as key actors in the supply of financial reporting information. All had substantial experience in accounting for R&D. Interviewees were drawn from a range of countries reporting under International Financial Reporting Standards, which could help minimise potential bias arising from country-specific factors. An iterative interpretative thematic approach was followed for the analysis of the interview data employing ambiguity aversion. Findings Preparers and auditors portray a tendency to expensing. This finding is consistent with ambiguity aversion where individuals act as if they take a worst-case outcome and a fear of negative evaluation regarding future impairments. Moreover, this sheds light on the findings of archival studies as to a relative lack of capitalisation. Further, the findings show that the accounting treatment of development costs can be viewed as being a dialogic social construction between preparers and auditors. Practical implications This research raises important policy implications and informs the International Accounting Standards Board's (IASB) current project to comprehensively review IAS 38. Originality/value The findings advance the financial accounting literature in relation to R&D and the consideration of ambiguity and ambiguity aversion in accounting practice. Prior accounting-related studies considering ambiguity have primarily adopted an experimental design often in a training environment with students. In contrast, this research directly reports the views of highly experienced auditors and preparers regarding a key and highly topical, accounting issue.

papers.title: Converging standards, diverging outcomes? An empirical analysis of interoperability in sustainability reporting
papers.abstract: Purpose This article investigates the evolving sustainability reporting landscape in the European Union (EU) following the implementation of the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). It explores the degree of interoperability – that is, the effective alignment between the ESRS and major international frameworks, including the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and the International Sustainability Reporting Standards (IFRS) – and evaluates how companies respond in practice. Design/methodology/approach The study conducts a comparative analysis of energy companies operating within the EU. The empirical analysis is supported by the construction of an interoperability grid and the subsequent measurement of interoperability indicators. Findings The analysis reveals strong alignment in disclosures between companies reporting under the ESRS and those reporting under the GRI, supporting the practical effectiveness of interoperability initiatives. In contrast, IFRS-aligned firms exhibit significantly lower and more heterogeneous disclosure levels, particularly in governance, highlighting limitations of investor-centric reporting frameworks in achieving comprehensive sustainability transparency. Research limitations/implications The findings are based on a cross-sectional sample from a single EU sector, limiting their generalisability. Nevertheless, the results inform policymakers and firms by evidencing practical interoperability between the ESRS and GRI while highlighting gaps in IFRS-aligned disclosures. Practical implications By empirically examining interoperability in practice, this study provides evidence-based insights for policymakers, standard setters, and firms, supporting alignment strategies and informing the implementation of sustainability reporting frameworks within the evolving EU regulatory landscape. Social implications Achieving a truly harmonised reporting environment across the EU would strengthen stakeholder trust, enhance the comparability of disclosures, and support effective and sustainable economic development. Originality/value This study provides empirical evidence on interoperability across the ESRS, GRI, and IFRS frameworks, offering one of the first disclosure-based assessments of cross-framework alignment in the early implementation phase of the CSRD.

papers.title: Determinants of green behaviour in the finance sector: moderating role of environmentally-specific servant leadership
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines the moderating role of Environmentally-Specific Servant Leadership (ESSL) on factors influencing green behaviour among internal stakeholders in the finance sector. The factors considered are attitude, concern, and knowledge about the environment, and perceived corporate social responsibility (CSR). Design/methodology/approach Two independent studies, involving students (n = 256) and employees (n = 233) in the financial sector, were conducted. Structural Equation Modelling was employed to test the hypothesised relationships, and a multi-group analysis was performed to compare results across the two samples. Findings The antecedents had a significant positive impact on green behaviour in both groups. ESSL was found to positively moderate the relationship between some of the antecedents and green behaviour, specifically, environmental attitude for students and perceived CSR for employees, amplifying their effect on green behaviour. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to two specific stakeholder groups within the finance sector, which may limit the generalisability of the findings to other sectors or stakeholder categories. Future research could extend this model to other industries and stakeholder groups to test the robustness of the moderating role of ESSL. Practical implications The findings have implications for policy formulation, curriculum development, and human resource strategies aimed at strengthening pro-environmental conduct among employees and future finance professionals. Originality/value The study extends the concept of respect in the finance sector beyond ethical conduct and fiduciary responsibility to environmental stewardship. By comparing the moderating effect of ESSL across two distinct internal stakeholder groups, it offers insight into how leadership shapes pro-environmental behaviour.

papers.title: Foundational perspectives on conceptual frameworks for accounting standards: advancing toward a meta-framework
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the conceptual fragmentation within the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) Conceptual Framework (CF) by investigating the interrelationships among three fundamental accounting choices: accounting approaches (balance sheet vs. income statement), capital maintenance concepts (financial vs. physical), and measurement bases (historical cost vs. current value). It aims to develop a comprehensive meta-framework that integrates these elements through broader foundational perspectives. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a normative methodology, the study synthesizes existing theoretical debates and formalizes alternative accounting positions. Through logical analysis, it identifies consistent configurations among the three accounting choices and organizes them into three overarching foundational perspectives: market, entrepreneurial, and institutional. Findings The research demonstrates that coherent links exist among accounting approaches, capital maintenance, and measurement bases. These are structured into three foundational perspectives, each representing a distinct accounting philosophy aligned with different stakeholder needs and epistemological views. The study proposes a meta-framework that integrates these perspectives to enhance conceptual coherence and regulatory flexibility. Research limitations/implications The study is theoretical and lacks empirical validation. Further research is needed to test the applicability of the meta-framework across diverse institutional and cultural contexts and to empirically assess the role of the institutional perspective in CFs. Practical implications The framework helps standard setters, policymakers, and managers tailor accounting practices and regulations to varied stakeholder interests and organizational contexts, improving transparency and relevance in financial reporting. Originality/value The study introduces a novel meta-framework that reinterprets foundational accounting choices through integrated perspectives, offering a more pluralistic and inclusive vision for CFs.

papers.title: Preventing recurring material misstatements through behavioural sustainment: a 5S-based conceptual framework for financial reporting
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper develops a conceptual framework to explain how behavioural discipline is sustained in routine financial reporting work and how such sustainment conditions the recurrence of material misstatements under conditions of reasonable assurance. Rather than treating reporting reliability as an outcome optimised through technical rules or ex post detection, the paper reconceptualises financial reporting as a behaviourally enacted process shaped by routines, accountability, and reinforcement over time. Design/methodology/approach The paper adopts a structured conceptual integration of accounting, management control and behavioural literature. The 5S principles – Sort, Set in Order, Shine, Standardise and Sustain – are reinterpreted as a behavioural process framework that explicates how reporting routines are enacted, coordinated, scrutinised and reinforced across reporting cycles. The approach is conceptual in nature and does not constitute a systematic review or a design science intervention. Findings The framework suggests that the recurrence of material misstatements is shaped less by the presence of additional procedures than by the extent to which disciplined reporting practices are behaviourally sustained over time. It explicates how 5S operates through behavioural mechanisms – such as selective attention to materiality, anticipatory coordination, anomaly questioning, accountable judgement and reinforcement across cycles – that condition how formal reporting requirements are enacted in practice, without assuming the elimination of judgement or error. Research limitations/implications As a conceptual paper, the framework does not provide empirical evidence of effectiveness and is developed primarily from literature grounded in regulated reporting environments. Practical implications The paper offers accountants, auditors, boards and regulators a conceptual lens for interpreting whether reporting routines are behaviourally sustained or have become symbolic, without implying a prescriptive intervention. Originality/value The paper reframes misstatement prevention as a problem of behavioural sustainment rather than technical optimisation, enabling recurring reporting failures to be analysed as manifestations of instability in routine enactment rather than isolated procedural deficiencies.

papers.title: Environmental taxes, CO2 emissions, and economic growth: evidence on the moderating role of institutional quality in developing countries
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines the heterogeneous effects of environmental taxes and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions on economic growth and investigates whether institutional quality conditions these relationships across developing economies. Design/methodology/approach Using an unbalanced panel dataset of 55 developing countries during 2010–2022, this study applies panel quantile regression and conducts robustness analyses using alternative estimation approaches. Findings First, environmental taxes negatively affect economic growth, with stronger adverse effects at higher growth quantiles. Second, CO2 emissions exhibit a positive and relatively stable association with economic growth, suggesting continued dependence on carbon-intensive production structures. Third, institutional quality strengthens the negative effect of environmental taxes at lower growth levels but mitigates this effect at higher growth levels. Finally, institutional quality weakens the positive relationship between CO2 emissions and economic growth across growth distributions. Research limitations/implications This study provides theoretical insights into how institutional quality shapes the growth effects of environmental taxation and environmental pressure across different growth conditions. Practical implications The findings suggest that improving institutional quality may help reduce the economic costs associated with environmental taxation while supporting more balanced economic and environmental policy implementation in developing economies. Originality/value This study extends the literature by demonstrating that the economic effects of environmental taxation and environmental pressure are not uniform across growth conditions but depend on institutional quality, thereby providing new evidence on the institutional conditions under which environmental policies influence economic growth.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: Digital transformation and workforce resilience in social enterprises: governance for crisis readiness
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how digital transformation, workforce resilience and governance integration influence crisis readiness in social enterprises. It explores capability-building as a potential mechanism connecting digital transformation and governance with crisis readiness, while governance maturity and ecosystem collaboration are considered contextual conditions that may shape these relationships. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative design combined a comprehensive literature review of forty peer-reviewed studies with six semi-structured interviews involving governance, workforce and digital transformation leaders. Inductive coding identified three themes: governance for crisis readiness, digital transformation enablers and workforce resilience routines, interpreted through institutional theory and dynamic capability theory. Findings Governance embedded in digital workflows strengthens reliability and accountability. Capability-building routines such as micro-drills, peer learning, and digital literacy translate strategy into continuity outcomes. Ecosystem partnerships and institutional maturity amplify these effects by improving interoperability, resource sharing and collective learning. Practical implications Integrating governance controls within digital systems and aligning workforce development with feedback and monitoring enhances readiness, transparency and long-term sustainability. Originality/value This study develops a mechanism-informed conceptual framework that integrates governance maturity, digital transformation and workforce capability to explain potential pathways toward crisis readiness in social enterprises. It identifies capability-building as a proposed explanatory mechanism and ecosystem conditions as contextual influences, offering an integrative foundation for future empirical testing.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: Exploring the local government accounting literacy of accounting teachers in a developing country
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to explore local government accounting (LGA) literacy among accounting teachers in a developing-country context. However, given the limited literature that provides instruments to assess accounting teachers' LGA literacy, this study develops an assessment instrument grounded in Bloom's Taxonomy and the Theory of Attitude and Attitude Change to achieve its aim. Design/methodology/approach Given the limited scholarly attention to assessing LGA literacy among accounting teachers, this study employed an exploratory approach using a quantitative descriptive method. First, an instrument for assessing LGA literacy was developed. Second, accounting teachers' LGA literacy was assessed within the context of vocational accounting teachers in the Daerah Istimewa Yogyakarta (DIY) Province, Indonesia. Third, the instrument's validity and reliability were analysed. Fourth, the assessment results were further analysed. Findings Using the developed accounting teachers' LGA literacy assessment instrument, this study reveals that accounting teachers in DIY Province, as a proxy for Indonesia, exhibit low levels of LGA literacy, primarily attributed to inadequate LGA knowledge. Further analysis indicates that limited LGA knowledge constrains teachers' recognition of LGA as an accountability instrument, which may weaken their attitudes towards LGA and subsequently reduce their engagement in LGA-related teaching practices. Originality/value This study addresses gaps in the existing literature in three ways. First, it provides evidence of the challenges faced by accounting teachers in delivering effective LGA instruction in a developing-country context. Second, it develops an instrument for assessing teachers' LGA literacy. Third, it demonstrates the theoretical integration of Bloom's Taxonomy and Attitude Change Theory in assessing and analysing accounting teachers' LGA literacy.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: Power, inclusion and the role of SMEs in European public procurement
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) participation in European public procurement, aiming to understand disparities across member states despite harmonised EU Directives. Design/methodology/approach Using a novel dataset of 839,778 tenders with information about SME participation from the Tenders Electronic Daily (TED) platform covering 29 countries from 2018 to 2023, we analyse SME participation rates, contract award shares, and geographic competition patterns. Findings Significant variation is observed: Eastern European countries exceed 80% SME participation, while several Western European countries remain below 40%. SMEs participate in about 80% of tenders but secure only 40–60% of contract values. Geographic proximity enhances SME competitiveness in local markets, especially for contracts under €500,000. Institutional and administrative factors appear more decisive than regulatory frameworks alone. Research limitations/implications Limitations include potential data quality issues. However, these were mitigated where possible, and the database remains the only available offering comparable data across Europe. Future research should explore institutional and cultural factors in greater depth through country-level studies. Practical implications Policymakers should adopt tailored approaches addressing administrative complexity and regional market conditions, simplifying procedures and improving data transparency to boost SME inclusion. Social implications Identifying ways to promote SME participation can support corrective actions that foster economic inclusion and strengthen local entrepreneurship across the EU. Originality/value This study provides new empirical evidence on the “implementation paradox” in EU public procurement, highlighting the need for context-specific strategies to enhance SME inclusion.
